reading.rtitle: The Night Ferry -- two hours, one kitchen, and a family that does not explain itself
paras: The Night Ferry is set in New Bedford, Massachusetts, in the summer of 1986, inside a Portuguese fishing family that had been in that town for three generations. The plot is simple enough to say in one line: a father goes out on the water one night and does not come back, and his nineteen-year-old daughter has to decide whether to sell the boat or take it out herself. Almost a third of the film is spoken in Portuguese, with subtitles, and nobody on screen apologizes for that. The cast is mostly unknown, which is the best decision the director made, because you believe these people when they work with their hands.

The first hour moves slowly, and it is supposed to. We had already been told, in the opening minutes, that the boat had been sold once before and bought back, so we watch a family argue about a decision they had made years earlier. Maria was working two jobs when the news arrived at the door; her brother was still at school and heard it from a neighbor. The director lets those scenes run to the end, and two people at my screening looked at their phones. Stay with it anyway. The film is slow-paced on purpose, because the second hour only works if you already know exactly how this family talks when nothing is wrong.

Then there is the twist, and I am not going to give away the ending. I will say only that it arrives in a kitchen, in a conversation that lasts about ninety seconds, and that it sends you back through the whole first hour again in your head. One detail is far-fetched: a letter turns up at exactly the right moment, and the film would be stronger without it. Everything else is earned. The score is the other surprise. There are no strings and no big emotional music, only a guitar and, twice, a radio playing in another room while somebody is doing the dishes.

So, is it worth two hours? Yes, and worth them in a cinema rather than at home, because half the work here is done by sound. Go to a subtitled screening even if you do not speak a word of Portuguese: the subtitles are part of the film, not a service added afterwards. There will be no sequel, and there should not be one, because this story finishes where it finishes. If you like films in which nothing explodes and everything matters, buy a ticket for one of the evening screenings this week, and do not read another word about it before you go.

listenings.text: Okay, so you have not seen it, and I am not going to give away the ending, I promise. It is set in a small port town on the coast, in the eighties, in a family that had been fishing there for three generations. The plot sounds like nothing when you say it out loud: the father goes out one night and does not come back. But here is the thing. While everybody was down at the water looking for the boat, the daughter opened his desk and found out that he had sold it, months before, and had never told anyone. And that is only forty minutes in. The first hour is slow-paced, I am not going to lie to you, but then there is a twist in a kitchen, of all places, and I actually said something out loud in the cinema. Just go. Do not read anything, do not watch the trailer, and do not let anybody tell you what happens at the end.

Good evening, and welcome. Tonight's feature is The Night Ferry, and this is the subtitled screening: part of the film is spoken in Portuguese and the subtitles on screen are in English. The seven fifteen screening is in Theater Four, up the stairs and to your left. The nine forty screening tonight is also in Theater Four, on the same floor. Please take a moment now to silence your phone. If your screen lights up during the film, an usher will come and ask you to put it away, and none of us wants that. There is no intermission. The running time is two hours and four minutes, and there is nothing after the credits, so you are free to leave when the lights come up. Restrooms are behind you, past the popcorn stand. Thank you, and enjoy the film.

People ask me this all the time, and my answer never changes: watch it subtitled. When a film is dubbed, the voice you are hearing was recorded in a studio months later by somebody who was never in that room, and you lose the exact thing you are trying to learn, which is how people sound when they interrupt each other, when they are tired, when they are lying. Subtitles are not cheating. They are a rope. So here is what I do. The first time through I read the subtitles and I let myself enjoy the plot. Then I go back to two or three scenes I liked and I watch them again with the subtitles off, two minutes each, that is all. And when the dialogue is too fast, and it will be, I stop trying to catch every single word and I listen for the three words that carry the meaning. You know, the ones you would have said yourself.
